rationale: B wins because it gives the founder one more real press shape: a buyer-level trade story, not just category chess. A's strongest frame, "Brex turns on local-currency cards in 50 countries because enterprises asked for one global spend stack," is sound but still talks like a market map; B's "The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" gives a concrete protagonist and a proof path an editor can picture. The headline overreaches on wires, but the body knows it needs a named customer and before/after proof.
gaps_in_A: "Story type: category-creation" overstates the news. Brex is expanding an existing corporate-card and spend-management product; the update does not prove a new category is being created.
"one global spend stack" is consultant fog. It is not fatal, but it is less human and less pitchable than a finance-team workflow story.

"Why local-currency reimbursement is the hard part of going global, not the card itself" asserts a hierarchy the facts do not prove. The update says local reimbursement exists, not that card issuance is easy.
"three viable shapes exist" misses the strongest trade path: a named customer with employees across regions explaining the before/after reimbursement mess.
gaps_in_B: "The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" invents the wire-transfer before-state. Good angle, sloppy headline.
"the wires, the FX losses, the month-end mess" stacks unproven pain points. Those belong in the proof request until a customer says them on record.
"opening a new front against Ramp and the banks" turns "traditional corporate-card issuers" into "banks." Probably directionally fair, but still a shorthand the update did not hand you.
"exec-spotlight" assumes there is a named product or payments executive with a build story. The set correctly asks for one, but the angle should stay conditional until that person exists.
